beats.intro: Module twelve. [[sub]]Convexity: the curve that duration alone misses, and how to measure the risk of a portfolio.
beats.convex: Duration is a straight line. The real price-yield relationship is a curve. [[a]]For small yield changes, the line is a good estimate. For large changes, it is not. [[b]]Convexity captures the curvature. [[f]]The improved estimate adds half the convexity, times the yield change squared, to the duration effect. [[ex]]Take the five year, three point two percent bond. Modified duration is four point five nine, and convexity is twenty four point two four. If the yield falls two points, the actual price gain is nine point six eight percent. Duration alone says nine point one seven. Adding convexity gives nine point six six. [[up]]If the yield rises two points, the actual change is minus eight point seven one. Duration alone says minus nine point one seven. With convexity, minus eight point six nine. [[pos]]For an option-free bond, convexity is always positive. Prices rise more when yields fall, and fall less when yields rise, than duration alone predicts.
beats.calc: Convexity can be approximated from prices. [[a]]Raise the yield five basis points, and lower it five basis points. [[b]]The new prices are one hundred point two three, and ninety nine point seven seven. [[f]]Convexity is the sum of these two prices, minus twice the original price, divided by the yield change squared, times the original price. [[res]]For this bond, that gives twenty four point two four.
beats.features: Convexity rises with longer maturity, with lower coupon, and with lower yield, just as duration does. [[bars]]For the same coupon and yield, a five year bond has convexity of about twenty four, a ten year bond eighty three, and a thirty year bond almost five hundred. [[disp]]The dispersion of cash flows also matters. Take two bonds with the same duration. The one whose cash flows are more spread out has more convexity. [[val]]With the same tangent line, the more convex bond gains more when yields fall, and loses less when they rise. So convexity is valuable, and a more convex bond is usually priced higher, with a lower yield.
beats.money: Money convexity does the same in currency. [[ex]]An investor holds fifty million pounds of a ten year, three point five percent bond at par. Modified duration is eight point three seven six, and convexity is eighty one point seven. [[dur]]Yields fall one percentage point. The duration effect is eight point three seven six percent. [[cvx]]The convexity adjustment is a half, times eighty one point seven, times point oh one squared. That is point four oh eight five percent. [[tot]]The total is eight point seven eight percent, a gain of about four point three nine million pounds. Convexity contributes about two hundred four thousand.
beats.portfolio: To measure a portfolio, there are two ways. [[a]]The theoretically correct way is the weighted average time to receipt of all the portfolio's cash flows. But it is hard to use. [[b]]The common way is the weighted average of each bond's duration and convexity. [[lim]]But it assumes parallel shifts in the yield curve, where all yields move by the same amount. Real curves rarely move that way. [[ex]]For example, take a portfolio with duration six point one six nine, and convexity fifty two point nine two one. If yields rise fifty basis points, the estimate is minus six point one six nine times point oh oh five, plus a half times fifty two point nine two one times point oh oh five squared. That is about minus three point oh two percent.
beats.wrap: Let's recap. [[w1]]Convexity captures the curvature that duration misses. [[w2]]Add half the convexity times the yield change squared to the duration effect. For an option-free bond, it always helps. [[w3]]Convexity is higher for longer, lower-coupon, lower-yield bonds, and more dispersed cash flows. [[w4]]Portfolio averages assume parallel shifts of the yield curve.
